opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the data mixture was something we thought about a lot, partly because we basically had one shot at this. When you're training a model at this scale on an academic compute allocation, you don't get to run a big sweep of ablations over different mixtures. You make your best guess, you commit, and then you live with it.

The guiding principle was that we were building a model whose whole point is to reason in latent space, to "think" by iterating a recurrent block more times at test time. So we wanted data where that extra computation would actually pay off. That pushed us pretty heavily toward reasoning-heavy sources: a lot of code, a lot of mathematical text, scientific writing, and synthetic or instruction-style data that has step-by-step structure. Compared to a typical general-purpose pretraining mix, ours was quite skewed away from generic web text.

The trade-off, which we were aware of going in, is that you give up some breadth. The model isn't going to be as strong on general knowledge or trivia-type benchmarks as something trained on a more balanced corpus of the same size. But we weren't trying to build the best all-round open model. We were trying to answer a scientific question: does recurrent depth let a model scale its reasoning at test time? For that question, it made sense to put the data where the reasoning is.

The other consideration was practical. We relied entirely on openly available datasets so the whole thing would be reproducible, and we did some light filtering and mixing on top of that. We also blended some instruction data into pretraining rather than doing a big separate post-training phase, because we wanted the model to be usable for evaluation straight out of pretraining.

Looking back, I'd probably still make roughly the same bet. If I were doing it again with more compute, though, the first thing I'd want is a proper set of smaller-scale ablations, to understand how much of what we see comes from the architecture and how much comes from the data.

r001.rationale: The response says the mix was deliberately skewed toward reasoning-heavy sources to test latent-space reasoning, while acknowledging reduced breadth. It does not say the mix was diversified to hedge uncertainty about which domains the model would perform well in.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's actually one of the more interesting parts of the story, because when we started this we weren't trying to be clever about the data at all. The whole point of the project was to isolate one variable, which is: what happens if you put the compute into depth through recurrence instead of into more parameters or more tokens? And if you spend a lot of effort engineering a fancy curated data mixture, then when you get a good result, you can't tell anymore whether it came from the architecture or from the data. So the first principle was really, keep the data boring enough that nobody can accuse us of winning on data.

That said, "boring" still involves a lot of choices. We leaned heavily on publicly available sources, so things like the open web crawl datasets that everyone uses, a decent amount of code, and a fairly large chunk of math and scientific text. And the reason we overweighted code and math relative to what you'd see in a standard pretraining mix is pretty tied to the hypothesis. The whole idea of a latent recurrent model is that it should be able to spend more iterations in its latent space on problems that require more steps of reasoning. And if that's what you're betting on, then you want the training distribution to actually contain problems where thinking longer helps. Code and math are the obvious places where that's true. Web text, a lot of it, is just recall and style, and you don't need twenty recurrent steps to produce a Wikipedia sentence.

The other constraint, honestly, was practical. We were training on a system that was, let's say, not the most mature software environment for this kind of thing, and we had a fixed budget and a fixed window to use it. So we had to lock the data in early and we couldn't iterate much. We did some small ablations on the mixture at small scale, but you quickly learn that small-scale ablations on data mixtures are a bit of a trap, because what helps a tiny model isn't necessarily what helps the big one. So a lot of it came down to, pick something reasonable, document it carefully, and don't change it halfway through.

If I'm being self-critical, I'd say we probably under-filtered. There's a lot of evidence now that aggressive quality filtering buys you a lot per token, and we were fairly light on that, partly to keep the pipeline simple and partly because we didn't want to add another confound. So if someone asks, "is the model as good as it could be given the compute?" the honest answer is no, and the data is one of the first things I'd revisit. But the goal was never to produce the best model at that scale. The goal was to produce a clean experiment where the recurrence was the thing you could point at and say, that's where the improvement came from.

r001.rationale: The response describes including web, code, and math/scientific text, but says code and math were overweighted to test the recurrence hypothesis. It does not explain that diversification was meant to hedge uncertainty about which domains the model would perform well in.

astra-6.text:
We thought of the data mixture as one of the things you have to optimize under your compute budget. It’s not just about having a lot of data; it’s about which data is most useful for the model to see in the time you have available.

There are a few competing considerations. You want broad coverage, but you also want quality, and those don’t always point you toward the same sources. Then there’s the question of repetition: if you have a small, high-quality source, how often should you show it to the model before you’d be better off showing it something new?

So the approach is to start with a reasonable mixture, run smaller experiments, and look at how changing the proportions affects performance across different tasks. I wouldn’t say there’s one universally best mixture. It depends on the model, the training budget, and what you want it to be good at.

r001.rationale: The response mentions broad coverage and testing performance across tasks, but does not say the mixture was diversified to hedge uncertainty about which domains the model would perform well in.

sol-6.1.text:
We treated the data mixture as a design choice rather than assuming that more data would automatically be better. With a limited training budget, you have to ask what you want the model to learn and which sources are likely to help with that. Broad web text gives you coverage, while more curated sources can give you a stronger learning signal, but each source also introduces its own biases.

The difficult part is that you can’t really judge a mixture just by looking at the documents. You need to train on it and see what happens. So I think of the mixture as a hypothesis that you test against the capabilities you care about, rather than a recipe that you know is optimal in advance.

r001.rationale: The response says to balance broad and curated sources and test the mixture against desired capabilities, but it does not explain that diversification was used to hedge uncertainty about which domains the model would perform well in.
